A pH- and Temperature-Dependent Cycling Method That
Doubles the Yield of Microtubule Protein

Suresh C. Tiwari! and Kathy A. Suprenant®

Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas 66045

Received May 10,1989

is report describes a procedure for the isolation of
microtubules (MTs) and microtubule-associated pro-
teins from mammalian cultured cells and tissues. This
method relies on the discovery that the solubility of
brain tubulin is pH-sensitive. In this report, we exam-
ined tubulin solubility over abroad pH range and discov-
ered that the amount of soluble tubulin increased by
240% as the pH was raised from 6.0 to 8.0. Quantitative
immunoblotting revealed that there was an almost
‘equal partitioning of tyrosinated and acetylated a-tubu-
lin isotypes at the higher pH. These observations were
incorporated into a new procedure for the purification
of microtubule protein (MTP) from bovine brain and
‘mouse B16 cultured melanoma cells. Morphologically
and in terms of polypeptide composition, this MTP is
indistinguishable from that prepared by a glycerol-cy-
cling method (21). Moreover, our new method of pH-
and temperature-cycling yields almost twice as much
MTP as that obtained by other cycling methods. « 1903

‘The molecular complexity of a microtubule lies some-
where between that of a ribosome and that of a mito-
chondrion (15,17). Presumably, this complexity is
needed for the wide variety of microtubule arrays that
perform many diverse functions such as membrane
trafficking and chromosome movements. One approach
to understanding how microtubules form and function
is to use purified microtubule components in reconst
tuted functional assays. This approach has been success-
ful in the identification and characterization of the mo-
tor protein, kinesin (28), and in the analysis of

‘Many methods have been successfully used for the
purification of microtubule protein. They fall into two
‘basic categories: those that rely on the self-assembly
properties of microtubules (5,21) and those that are in-
duced to assemble with the drug taxol (29). We report
here on an adaptation of a pH- and temperature-depen-
dent assembly/disassembly method for the purification
of brain microtubule protein. This method, originally
developed for purification of sea urchin tubulin by Su-
prenant and Marsh (1987), and now modified for brain
tissue, provides a significantly higher yield of appar-
ently normal microtubules from bovine brain. In addi-
tion, the slightly alkaline assembly buffer facilitates
polymerization of microtubules from crude extracts at
low temperatures (24°C) which is appropriate for tis:
‘sues isolated from cold-blooded animals or extracts that
contain proteolytic activity. This method is rapid and
does not require the use of an ultracentrifuge.

MATERIALS AND METHODS.
Preparation of Extracts for pH Solubility Experiments

Bovine brain extracts (100,000g supernatants) were
prepared in the following manner. Whole brains were
transported on ice from a nearby slaughterhouse and
rinsed once in ice-cold 0.8% NaCl. Pia and blood vessels
were removed from the chilled brain. The brain was
rinsed once in fresh ice-cold 0.8% NaCl, and again in
